title: Searching for Sasquatch: Bigfoot Townhall descends on UVic
excerpt: They walk among us. You just can’t necessarily tell one by looking.
content:
They walk among us. You just can’t necessarily tell one by looking.

“I wouldn’t look at you and automatically assume you are someone who researches Bigfoot,” I told Alex Solunac, a Sasquatch researcher in Victoria.

“I don’t know what the typical Sasquatch researcher looks like,” he replied.

Fair enough.

If there’s a rule No. 1 in Sasquatch research, it might be: never assume.

Rule No. 2: Don’t call it Bigfoot. That’s American.

Here in Canada, we call it the Sasquatch. Or, at least, some of us do.

“If you really want to see a Sasquatch, I recommend driving around on logging roads at dusk,” Solunac said.

There are plenty of Sasquatch sighting videos from B.C. There are blurry figures, mysterious shapes and enough shaky forest footage to keep the internet occupied indefinitely.

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

What there isn’t is however, is the one thing that would settle the matter: conclusive proof.

That’s what Solunac and other Sasquatch researchers are looking for.

And on Thursday, they gathered at UVic for a discussion about the world’s foremost forest-dwelling loner.

“We’ve never done one of these in Victoria,” Solunac told me.

The event was actually called a Bigfoot town hall, because this particular production was American.

And Bigfoot, it turns out, is big business.

Earlier in the day, a Bigfoot-themed cruise arrived at Ogden Point from Alaska by way of Seattle. The passengers then headed to UVic to talk about the creature they believe could be hiding somewhere in the forests of the Pacific Northwest.

Adam Davies is a U.S.-based featured speaker at Thursday’s Townhall.

“I’ve already found evidence of him. I’ve seen him once but what we need to do is to get really good scientific evidence and that’s what we’re doing.”

As a reporter, that’s about as investigative as I get.

Since UVic has trees, I figured it was as fertile a hunting ground as any.

“Hey, wait. Is that proof of Bigfoot?” I asked Sofia, a graduate student after I spotted something resembling deer droppings on the ground.

“I’m sure his excrement would be way larger than that,” she replied.

Case closed.

What I expected to find on campus was a collection of logic-thirsty fact-o-holics. What I found was the opposite.

“I think it’s possible,” one student said.

“There’s a lot of forest out there,” another added.

“Do you want to believe in Bigfoot?” I asked a student name Giuseppe.

“Yeah,” he said.

Same.

And then there was David.

You can’t tell a Sasquatch believer just by looking at one, unless you’re looking at David.

“Man, I’m glad I ran into you,” I told him.

“Yeah, I’m glad to see you too,” he said, laughing.

David Dick’s truck makes no apologies about what he believes. It’s covered in decals declaring the existence of the Sasquatch. The stickers are one thing, but experience is another.

He got hooked on Sasquatch after he experienced the presence of something mysterious by the river near the home of his late grandparents.

“All my hairs were standing up on the back of my neck,” David recalled. “And I was like, ‘Ooh, this doesn’t feel right.’”

It’s a feeling he says he hasn’t been able to shake his entire life.

And maybe that’s where belief in Sasquatch begins.

Not with a laboratory or a DNA sample.

With that one strange moment when you saw something, heard something or felt something you simply couldn’t explain.

Millions of people, over hundreds of years, have reported something similar.

How could they all be wrong?

Well, they could, but the search will continue regardless.

“My belief is just that it’s an undocumented animal,” says Solunac. “It leaves tracks. We’ve found hair samples. All this kind of stuff.”

The only problem with undocumented hair samples is there’s no match out there. “We can’t match it to something because we don’t have a dead Sasquatch,” he says.

No accepted DNA sample. No body sitting in a freezer somewhere waiting to end the debate.

The search continues.
